Add all users to the local Administrators group

explanation.correct: A BIOS/UEFI supervisor (setup) password prevents unauthorized users from changing firmware settings such as boot order or enabling external boot, which would otherwise let them bypass the OS and its protections.

distractors.A: BitLocker To Go encrypts removable drives; it doesn't stop someone from changing the firmware boot order.
distractors.B: Disabling the firewall removes a protective control — it weakens security rather than hardening it.
distractors.D: Adding users to Administrators violates least privilege and makes the system less secure, not more.

explanation.exam_pattern: Lock down boot order / external boot = BIOS/UEFI (supervisor) password.

questions.stem: A technician is configuring a password policy to harden user accounts. Which TWO settings reflect password best practices? (Choose two.)

options.text: Set passwords to expire and require periodic change
Require a minimum length and complexity (mix of character types)
Store all user passwords in a shared spreadsheet for recovery
Disable account lockout so users are never locked out

explanation.correct: Enforcing a minimum length with complexity and requiring periodic expiration/change are standard password-hardening practices that resist guessing and limit how long a compromised password stays useful.

distractors.C: Storing passwords in a shared spreadsheet exposes every credential at once — a severe security failure, not a best practice.
distractors.D: Disabling account lockout lets attackers brute-force passwords with unlimited attempts; lockout thresholds should be ENABLED.

explanation.exam_pattern: Harden passwords: length + complexity, expiration, history, and account lockout; never store them in plaintext or remove lockout.

questions.stem: As part of account-management hardening on a new workstation, which action follows best practice?

options.text: Give every user membership in the Administrators group
Keep the manufacturer's default credentials on the device
Rename the default Administrator account and disable the Guest account
Leave the Guest account enabled for convenience

explanation.correct: Renaming the built-in Administrator account (so attackers can't target a known name) and disabling the Guest account reduce the attack surface — core account-management hardening steps.

distractors.A: Making every user an administrator violates least privilege and lets any user or their malware alter the system.
distractors.B: Keeping default credentials is a well-known risk; default usernames/passwords should always be changed.
distractors.D: Leaving Guest enabled provides an anonymous, low-control foothold; it should be disabled.

explanation.exam_pattern: Account hardening: rename/secure the default admin, disable Guest, change default credentials, apply least privilege.

questions.stem: Which ongoing practice BEST protects workstations against exploitation of newly discovered operating-system and application vulnerabilities?

options.text: Running as a local administrator at all times
Disabling automatic updates to avoid reboots
Patch/update management — keep the OS and applications current

explanation.correct: Patch (update) management — regularly applying OS and application updates/security patches — closes known vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them, and is a fundamental hardening practice.

distractors.A: Running as administrator all the time violates least privilege and lets malware make system-wide changes.
distractors.B: Turning off the host firewall removes a protective control and exposes the machine to network attacks.
distractors.C: Disabling automatic updates leaves known vulnerabilities unpatched, directly increasing risk.

explanation.exam_pattern: Close known vulnerabilities = patch/update management; pair it with least privilege and a host firewall.

questions.stem: A company wants to permanently destroy the data on failed magnetic hard disk drives by exposing them to a powerful magnetic field. Which sanitization method is this?

explanation.correct: Degaussing uses a strong magnetic field to scramble the magnetic domains on a hard disk drive, destroying the data (and usually the drive). It works only on magnetic media.

distractors.A: A standard/quick format only clears the file table and leaves the underlying data recoverable — it isn't secure destruction.
distractors.C: A low-level format rewrites the drive's low-level structures but uses no magnetic field; it's a software/firmware operation and the term is often misused for a full overwrite.
distractors.D: Secure erase issues a firmware command to wipe a drive's cells (useful for SSDs/HDDs being kept for reuse); it's not a magnetic-field method.

explanation.exam_pattern: Strong magnetic field wiping a magnetic HDD = degaussing (no effect on SSDs/flash, which have no magnetic domains).

questions.stem: A drive will NOT be reused and its data must be physically destroyed. Which TWO are physical destruction methods? (Choose two.)

options.text: Deleting the files and emptying the Recycle Bin
Drilling or hammering through the platters

explanation.correct: Shredding and drilling/crushing the platters physically destroy the media so the data cannot be recovered — appropriate when the drive won't be reused.

distractors.A: Deleting files and emptying the Recycle Bin removes only pointers to the data, which is trivially recoverable.
distractors.C: A quick format only clears the file table; the underlying data remains recoverable, so it is neither physical destruction nor secure.

explanation.exam_pattern: Physical destruction = shred, drill/hammer, incinerate, degauss (magnetic); format/delete are NOT secure.

questions.stem: After paying a third-party vendor to destroy its decommissioned drives, a company needs documented proof — for auditors and compliance — that each drive was actually destroyed. What should the vendor provide?

explanation.correct: A certificate of destruction is the formal document a disposal/recycling vendor provides attesting that specific media were destroyed, giving an auditable record for compliance and chain of custody.

distractors.A: A warranty card covers hardware defects, not proof of data destruction.
distractors.C: A software license key is unrelated to proving that media was destroyed.
distractors.D: A format log wouldn't prove physical destruction, and a quick format isn't secure destruction anyway.

explanation.exam_pattern: Proof that an outsourced vendor destroyed media = certificate of destruction (supports chain of custody/compliance).

questions.stem: A company plans to REUSE a batch of working hard drives internally but must first ensure the previous department's data cannot be recovered. Which method is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Delete the partitions in Disk Management
Perform a drive wipe/secure erase that overwrites all sectors

explanation.correct: Because the drives will be reused, they should be sanitized (not destroyed): a drive wipe/secure erase overwrites every sector so prior data is unrecoverable while keeping the drive usable.

distractors.A: Deleting partitions removes volume structures but leaves the underlying data recoverable.
distractors.B: A quick format only clears the file table; the data remains and can be recovered.
distractors.D: Shredding destroys the drives — appropriate for disposal, not when the hardware must be reused.

explanation.exam_pattern: Reuse the drive -> sanitize (wipe/secure erase/overwrite); dispose of the drive -> physically destroy (shred/drill/degauss/incinerate).

questions.stem: A desktop that worked yesterday now halts at boot with 'BOOTMGR is missing — Press Ctrl+Alt+Del to restart.' No hardware was changed and the drive is still detected in BIOS/UEFI. What is the BEST way to fix it?

options.text: Boot the Windows installation/recovery media into the Windows Recovery Environment and run Startup Repair or bootrec /rebuildbcd and bootrec /fixboot
Run sfc /scannow from within the running desktop
Replace the hard drive and reinstall Windows from scratch

explanation.correct: The boot manager/BCD files are missing or corrupt. Boot into WinRE from installation or recovery media and repair the boot files with Startup Repair or the bootrec commands (/fixboot, /rebuildbcd). The drive is healthy (detected in firmware), so nothing needs replacing.

distractors.B: You cannot run sfc from the desktop because the PC won't boot to it, and sfc repairs protected system files, not the BCD/boot sector.
distractors.C: Reseating RAM addresses memory faults (POST failures/BSODs), not a missing boot manager.
distractors.D: The drive is detected and otherwise fine; replacing it is drastic and destroys data when only the boot files are broken.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'BOOTMGR is missing' / 'No OS found' with the drive detected -> boot WinRE and rebuild boot files (Startup Repair, bootrec /fixboot and /rebuildbcd).

questions.stem: A technician runs sfc /scannow, but it reports 'Windows Resource Protection found corrupt files but was unable to fix some of them.' The component store itself is damaged. Which command should be run NEXT so SFC can then succeed?

explanation.correct: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth repairs the Windows component store (WinSxS) using Windows Update as the source; after it completes, re-running sfc /scannow can fix the protected files it previously couldn't.

distractors.B: bootrec repairs boot configuration data, which is unrelated to SFC's component store.
distractors.C: diskpart clean wipes the partition table and data — destructive and completely wrong here.
distractors.D: chkdsk repairs file-system/disk errors, not a corrupt Windows component store.

explanation.exam_pattern: SFC can't repair -> repair the image with DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth, then re-run sfc /scannow.

questions.stem: After a sudden power loss, a Windows PC shows repeated errors about missing or corrupt system DLLs and some built-in apps won't open, but the PC still boots. Which built-in tool should the technician run FIRST to verify and repair protected OS files?

explanation.correct: System File Checker (sfc /scannow) scans all protected operating-system files and replaces corrupted ones with known-good cached copies — the right first repair for corrupt/missing system files when the OS still boots.

distractors.B: Device Manager manages hardware and drivers, not the integrity of system files.
distractors.C: Disk Cleanup deletes temporary files to free space; it does not repair system files.
distractors.D: Formatting C: erases the OS and data — far too drastic for repairable file corruption.

explanation.exam_pattern: Corrupt/missing protected OS files but the PC still boots -> sfc /scannow first (then DISM if SFC can't fix them).

questions.stem: A Windows 11 laptop became unstable right after a batch of updates and a new application were installed. The user needs the OS returned to the way it worked yesterday WITHOUT losing personal documents. What is the BEST option?

options.text: Use System Restore to roll back to a restore point from before the changes
Perform a full factory reset that removes everything

explanation.correct: System Restore reverts system files, drivers, the registry, and installed programs/updates to an earlier restore point while leaving personal files intact — ideal for undoing recent destabilizing changes.

distractors.B: Defragmenting reorganizes files on disk for performance; it does not undo problematic updates or applications.
distractors.C: Deleting the profile destroys the user's settings and data and still doesn't roll back the system changes.
distractors.D: A factory reset that removes everything would wipe the user's documents — the opposite of the requirement.

explanation.exam_pattern: Undo recent bad updates/apps but keep user files -> System Restore (restore point); reset/reimage only when restore can't recover it.

questions.stem: A workstation reboots instantly whenever a blue screen occurs, so the technician can't read the STOP code. Which change lets them see the BSOD details on screen before it reboots?

options.text: In System Properties > Advanced > Startup and Recovery, clear the 'Automatically restart' checkbox
Enable Fast Startup in Power Options

explanation.correct: Clearing 'Automatically restart' under Startup and Recovery (System failure) keeps the blue screen displayed instead of instantly rebooting, so the STOP code/driver can be recorded. The same details are also written to Event Viewer and the memory dump.

distractors.A: BitLocker encrypts the drive; it doesn't affect crash-display behavior.
distractors.C: Enlarging the page file can allow a larger dump, but it does not stop the auto-reboot that hides the STOP code.
distractors.D: Fast Startup speeds boot via a hybrid shutdown; it has nothing to do with showing BSOD details.

explanation.exam_pattern: Can't read the STOP code because it reboots instantly -> disable 'Automatically restart' (Startup and Recovery), or read the dump/Event Viewer.

questions.stem: A PC suffers random freezes the technician suspects are caused by one of many third-party background services or startup items. Which tool starts Windows with non-Microsoft services and startup items disabled (a 'clean boot') to isolate the culprit?

explanation.correct: System Configuration (msconfig) performs a clean/diagnostic boot — on the Services tab you 'Hide all Microsoft services' and disable the rest, then re-enable items in batches to find the offending service.

distractors.A: Disk Management handles partitions and volumes, not which services and startup items load.
distractors.C: Resource Monitor shows live CPU/disk/network/memory usage but doesn't disable services for a clean boot.
distractors.D: Registry Editor edits registry keys directly; it is not the tool for performing a controlled clean boot.

explanation.exam_pattern: Isolate a third-party service/startup conflict -> msconfig clean/diagnostic boot; startup apps themselves are managed in Task Manager > Startup.

questions.stem: A Windows PC has been crashing intermittently over the past week. Which TWO built-in tools BEST help the technician review a history of the errors and correlate them with recent software changes? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: Event Viewer logs detailed system/application errors and warnings over time, and Reliability Monitor presents a day-by-day stability timeline that lines crashes up with installs and updates — together they pinpoint when and why the instability began.

distractors.B: Disk Management manages partitions and volumes and provides no crash or error log.
distractors.C: Disk Cleanup only deletes temporary files to reclaim space; it keeps no error history.

explanation.exam_pattern: Review crash history and correlate with changes -> Event Viewer (logs) + Reliability Monitor (stability timeline).

questions.stem: On one PC, typing a well-known banking URL loads a convincing fake site, yet other computers reach the real site and this PC's DNS settings look normal. Which file has MOST likely been altered by malware to redirect the domain?

explanation.correct: A malicious entry in the local hosts file maps the bank's domain to an attacker's IP, so that one PC is redirected regardless of DNS. Inspect and clean the hosts file and scan for malware.

distractors.A: pagefile.sys is virtual-memory swap space; editing it would not redirect a website.
distractors.C: The SAM stores local account password hashes; it doesn't map hostnames to addresses.
distractors.D: boot.ini is a legacy boot-configuration file (pre-Vista); it plays no part in name resolution or redirection.

explanation.exam_pattern: One PC redirected to a fake site while DNS is fine -> check the hosts file for malicious entries.

questions.stem: A pop-up covering the screen warns 'Windows detected 5 viruses! Call 1-800-XXX-XXXX or click here to buy FullCleanPro now.' The user never installed that program. What should the technician do?

options.text: Call the number so the viruses get removed quickly
Treat it as a fake/rogue antivirus (scareware): don't call or pay, and remove the malware with legitimate anti-malware (in Safe Mode if needed)
Ignore it; genuine Windows Security pop-ups always include a payment link
Purchase the advertised program to clear the alert

explanation.correct: Unsolicited 'pay now / call this number' virus warnings are classic rogue antivirus/scareware. Don't engage or pay; remove the underlying malware with a trusted anti-malware tool, booting to Safe Mode or a preinstallation environment if it blocks you.

distractors.A: The number reaches the scammers, who will try to extract money or remote access — never call it.
distractors.C: Legitimate Windows Security alerts never demand payment or a phone call; that wording is a red flag, not proof of authenticity.
distractors.D: Paying rewards the attacker and does not clean the system; the 'product' is fraudulent.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Pay now / call this number' virus warning = rogue AV/scareware -> don't pay or call; remove with legitimate anti-malware.

questions.stem: A user reports constant browser pop-ups, and now Task Manager, Registry Editor, and UAC prompts are all disabled with 'disabled by your administrator' messages — though no admin made those changes. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: A malware infection that disabled the security/management tools to protect itself

explanation.correct: Malware commonly disables Task Manager, regedit, and UAC (and throws pop-ups) to keep the user from inspecting or stopping it. The combination of symptoms points to infection; begin the malware-removal procedure.

distractors.B: A failing drive causes slow access, read errors, or boot failure — not disabled management tools and pop-ups.
distractors.C: An old GPU driver may cause display glitches or BSODs, not disabled Task Manager/regedit/UAC with pop-ups.
distractors.D: A dead battery powers the device off; it doesn't selectively disable Windows security tools.

explanation.exam_pattern: Task Manager/regedit/UAC disabled + pop-ups = compromise -> start malware removal (Safe Mode / anti-malware).

questions.stem: After multiple anti-malware scans and removals, a PC keeps getting reinfected and still behaves abnormally; a rootkit is suspected. Per best practice, what is the MOST reliable way to return the system to a trusted state?

options.text: Reimage/reinstall the OS from known-good media and restore data from a clean backup
Run the same antivirus scan a fourth time
Hide the symptoms by disabling the alerts

explanation.correct: When malware — especially a rootkit — can't be reliably removed and symptoms persist, the trustworthy path is to wipe and reimage/reinstall the OS from known-good media and restore data from a clean backup.

distractors.B: Repeating the same scan that already failed is unlikely to remove a persistent rootkit.
distractors.C: Disabling alerts only hides symptoms while the infection remains active — it fixes nothing.
distractors.D: Replacing the power supply addresses a hardware/power fault, not a software compromise.

explanation.exam_pattern: Persistent/rootkit infection that won't clean -> reimage from known-good media and restore from a clean backup.

questions.stem: Several of a user's contacts report receiving spam 'from' the user, and the user's Sent folder contains messages they never wrote. Which response BEST addresses a likely compromised email account?

options.text: Change the account password to a strong, unique one, enable MFA, and scan the device for malware
Create a brand-new email address and abandon the old one without further action
Delete all of the user's contacts

explanation.correct: Spam sent from the account and unknown Sent items indicate a hijacked account. Regain control by setting a strong, unique password, enabling multifactor authentication, and scanning the device for credential-stealing malware.

distractors.A: Disabling the firewall reduces protection and does nothing to reclaim the compromised account.
distractors.C: Abandoning the address ignores the root cause (stolen credentials/malware) and loses the user's history.
distractors.D: Deleting contacts neither secures the account nor stops the attacker from using it.

explanation.exam_pattern: Account sending spam / unknown Sent mail = hijacked account -> change password, enable MFA, scan for malware.

questions.stem: Windows Update repeatedly fails to install with an error, and the problem persists across reboots. Which step is the BEST first fix?

options.text: Run the Windows Update troubleshooter, then reset the update components by stopping the services and clearing the SoftwareDistribution cache
Disconnect the PC from the Internet permanently

explanation.correct: For failing updates, start with the built-in Windows Update troubleshooter; if it persists, reset the update components by stopping the update services and clearing the SoftwareDistribution download cache so the files are re-fetched cleanly.

distractors.B: Reinstalling Windows is far too drastic as a first response to an update error.
distractors.C: A failing system board doesn't present as Windows Update errors; replacing it is unjustified.
distractors.D: Disconnecting from the Internet makes updating impossible instead of fixing the failure.

explanation.exam_pattern: Updates fail with an error -> Windows Update troubleshooter, then reset components (clear SoftwareDistribution) before any drastic step.

questions.stem: In CompTIA's malware-removal procedure, the technician disables System Restore on a Windows PC before remediating. Why is this step important?

options.text: Disabling it speeds up the CPU during scanning
System Restore permanently deletes user documents if left enabled
Restore points can contain the malware, so a later restore could reinfect the system; disabling it purges those infected points
System Restore prevents antivirus software from installing

explanation.correct: Malware can be captured inside restore points; rolling back later would reintroduce the infection. Disabling System Restore before remediation purges those infected points, so you re-enable it and create a fresh, clean restore point afterward.

distractors.A: Toggling System Restore has no effect on CPU speed.
distractors.B: System Restore does not delete personal documents; it reverts system files and settings, not user data.
distractors.D: System Restore does not block antivirus installation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Disable System Restore during malware removal so infected restore points can't reinfect; re-enable and make a clean point at the end.

questions.stem: A user's smartphone has a bulging back cover, and the screen is being pushed up by a swollen battery. What is the correct action?

options.text: Puncture the battery to release the built-up gas
Put the phone in a freezer and continue charging it
Power the device down, stop charging/using it, do NOT puncture it, and have the swollen battery safely replaced and recycled
Press the battery back into place and keep using the phone

explanation.correct: A swollen lithium-ion battery is a fire/rupture hazard. Power off, stop charging and using it, avoid any pressure, and never puncture it; have it replaced and recycled through proper channels.

distractors.A: Puncturing a lithium battery can make it ignite or explode and releases hazardous chemicals — extremely dangerous.
distractors.B: Freezing and continuing to charge a damaged battery adds thermal and electrical stress and does not make it safe.
distractors.D: Forcing a swollen battery back into place stresses it further and risks rupture or fire.

explanation.exam_pattern: Swollen/bulging battery -> stop using, power off, do NOT puncture, replace and recycle safely.

questions.stem: On an otherwise healthy phone, one app repeatedly crashes or fails to load while every other app works fine. What is the BEST first troubleshooting step for that app?

options.text: Immediately perform a full factory reset of the phone
Force close the app and update it; if it still fails, clear its cache/data or uninstall and reinstall it

explanation.correct: When a single app misbehaves, target that app: force stop it, install any update, and if needed clear its cache/data (Android) or delete and reinstall it. This resolves most app-specific corruption without touching the rest of the device.

distractors.A: A screen swap is a hardware fix unrelated to a single app crashing.
distractors.B: A factory reset wipes the whole device and user data — far too drastic for one misbehaving app.
distractors.D: Turning off cellular doesn't fix app-file corruption and disables connectivity the app may need.

explanation.exam_pattern: One app crashing while others work -> update/force stop, then clear its cache/data or reinstall; reset the whole device only as a last resort.

questions.stem: A smartphone is completely frozen — the touchscreen won't respond and no button brings up any menu. What should the technician try FIRST?

options.text: Let the battery fully drain over several days
Factory reset the device from a computer
Perform a forced restart (soft reset), e.g., holding the power and volume buttons until it reboots

explanation.correct: A forced restart (soft reset) — typically holding power plus a volume button — reboots a frozen device without erasing data and clears the temporary hang. It is the correct, least-invasive first step.

distractors.A: Replacing the digitizer assumes a hardware fault before trying the quick software reset.
distractors.B: Waiting days for the battery to drain is impractical; a forced restart recovers it immediately.
distractors.C: A factory reset erases user data and is unnecessary for a simple freeze; try a forced restart first.

explanation.exam_pattern: Frozen/unresponsive phone -> forced restart (soft reset) first; factory reset only if the freezing keeps recurring.

questions.stem: A user can send and receive normal email on their phone but cannot open encrypted (S/MIME) messages, which show a decryption/certificate error. What is the MOST likely fix?

options.text: Install or renew the user's email encryption certificate (S/MIME digital certificate) on the device

explanation.correct: Opening S/MIME-encrypted mail requires the user's valid certificate (with its private key) on the device. A missing, expired, or not-yet-installed certificate causes the decryption error, so install or renew the S/MIME certificate.

distractors.A: Auto-rotate is a display setting unrelated to encryption.
distractors.C: Clearing the call log does not affect email certificates.
distractors.D: Screen brightness has nothing to do with decrypting email.

explanation.exam_pattern: Can't open encrypted (S/MIME) email -> missing/expired certificate; install or renew the email certificate on the device.

questions.stem: A user's phone won't connect to a new Bluetooth headset. Both devices are charged and nearby. Which step is MOST likely to establish the connection?

options.text: Put the headset into pairing/discoverable mode and pair it from the phone, removing any stale pairing and entering the PIN if prompted

explanation.correct: Bluetooth pairing requires the accessory to be in pairing/discoverable mode and within range; initiate pairing from the phone, and if a previous or partial pairing exists, 'forget' it and re-pair (supplying the PIN/passkey if asked).

distractors.A: The SIM card handles cellular service, not Bluetooth pairing.
distractors.C: Disabling Wi-Fi is unrelated to Bluetooth pairing and isn't required.
distractors.D: Airplane mode disables the radios, including Bluetooth, preventing any connection.

explanation.exam_pattern: Bluetooth won't connect -> put the accessory in pairing mode, ensure it's in range/discoverable, remove any stale pairing and re-pair (enter the PIN).

questions.stem: Right after a user sideloaded an app from an APK file obtained outside the official store, their phone shows a spike in data usage, a data-limit notification, and a flood of pop-up ads. Which TWO actions BEST remediate this likely malicious app? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run a reputable mobile anti-malware scan and review the app's permissions

explanation.correct: A sideloaded APK that triggers heavy data use and ad pop-ups is likely malware/adware. Remove the offending app and run a reputable mobile anti-malware scan, reviewing and revoking suspicious permissions to clean up anything it installed.

distractors.B: Raising the data cap just pays for the malware's traffic — it doesn't remove the threat.
distractors.D: Auto-rotate is a display setting and has nothing to do with the malicious app's data/ad behavior.

explanation.exam_pattern: High data use + ads after sideloading an APK = mobile malware/adware -> uninstall the app and run anti-malware / check permissions (avoid sideloading).
